newsitem.title: UK: Foreign investors eager to buy Russian risk.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investors eager to buy Russian risk.

text.p: Despite the politicking in the Kremlin and continued worries over President Boris Yeltsin's health, foreign investors remain hungry for Russian assets.

The sacking by Yeltsin of security supremo Alexander Lebed on Thursday came at a crucial time for Russia as it prepares for a huge foray into western capital markets with a $460 million global share offer from natural gas giant RAO Gazprom next week and up to $500 million in a Eurobond issue.
"While it is too early to comment on the timing of the Eurobond, it is clear that potential investors are aware of the risks involved in Russia," said a banker close to the deal.
The deal is believed to be set for the first week of November and analysts say that a five-year deal could be priced at 350-400 basis points over the equivalent U.S. Treasuries.
The banker said that the positive credit rating news on Russia two weeks ago had created the conditions under which new investors would feel comfortable holding the country's debt.
"At BB-minus from Standard & Poors, Russia's foreign currency debt is rated more highly than Brazil," he added.
Some $32 billion of Russian foreign debt is in the process of being restructured by commercial bank creditors.
"The deal has critical mass and looks set to be completed before the end of the year," said Philip Poole, chief east Europe economist at ING Barings.
Direct foreign investment in the domestic bond market is more difficult to quantify, partly because there were a number of semi-legal schemes before the official opening.

Foreign investment in Russian GKO Treasury bill market was around $2.10 billion between August 15 and October 15, while from October 1 to 15, foreigners put $850-900 million in the OFZ, federal loan bonds, market compared with $350-$400 million in August.

Foreign penetration into the country's equity market has been more limited, mainly because there is very little liquidity. The market traded $47 million on its most active day on October 9 and the capitalisation of the RTS-24 index of leading shares is $21 billion.
Analaysts believe that $300 million in foreign money is invested directly in Russian securities listed in Moscow, mostly blue chip shares.

Gazprom's international issue will change that as investors will be able to access a market which is not tightly controlled and in which they can buy and sell dollar denominated securities which will be listed in London, thus avoiding the hassles of buying and selling shares in Moscow.

Lead managers Morgan Stanley and Kleinwort Benson have said that the issue will be priced at the equivalent of $1.40-$1.60 per underlying share, implying a market capitalisation for the world's largest natural gas company of $33.0-$38.0 billion, far more than the rest of the market put together.
Bankers say that so far foreign investors have been resilient despite repeated rumours that Yeltsin had already died, dark talk of army coups and the sacking of Lebed.

"If anything, yesterday's news strengthens the hand of reform. The wide range of investors who are looking at Gazprom are aware of the potential upside and downside of Russia," said one London-based banker familiar with Gazprom issue.
After a blip on Thursday, foreign investors resumed active buying of Russian shares listed overseas on Friday.
"We started seeing strong demand for Russian equity," said Patrick Shanahan, managing director of Societe Generale Emerging European Markets.
He believes the outlook is bright, despite any lingering worries over Yeltsin's health and that reforms will continue.

"Lebed is not going to cause trouble. He knows that if he wants to win any presidential election which is held in the eventuality of Yeltsin's death he must get on well with the business community," Shanahan added. -- David Chance London newsroom 44 171 542 5887
